criteria.name: brief_fidelity
criteria.description: The premise is recognizably the story the brief asked for — same subject matter, same kind of cast, same spirit. Test: if the brief asked for a family trip and the premise is a corporate conspiracy with a deadline, score 0–25. If someone reading only the premise could guess what the user asked for, score 70+.

criteria.name: central_question
criteria.description: The central_question is a collision between two things the protagonist genuinely values and cannot have at once — X or Y, where a thoughtful person could want either. Not a logistics problem (settled by competence or effort) and not a proposition with one obvious answer (where the losing side is undefendable). Test: 'Can she finish in time?' fails (0–35) — effort settles it, no values are in tension. 'Should she save the kids?' fails (0–35) — only a monster picks the other pole. 'Does the knight honor the oracle's acceptance of death, or fight for a life she has already surrendered?' passes (70+) — her agency and her life are both worth wanting, and reasonable people would split. The question must be one this premise's situation actually argues, not a bolted-on abstraction.

criteria.name: grimgong_test
criteria.description: Each character's situation reads as one particular person, not an archetype with adjectives. 'A gruff warrior haunted by war' fails (0–35); 'a purpose-bred imperial crusher; the war is over and the thing he was built for no longer exists' passes (70+). Specificity must come from the situation, not stacked adjectives. The charge field names something genuinely unresolved or magnetic, and no character exists merely to fill a plot function (no love-interest-by-quota, no designated villain without their own situation).

criteria.name: voice_specificity
criteria.description: Voice descriptions name concrete, imitable mechanics a writer could use to impersonate the character cold — vocabulary level, sentence length and rhythm, and what changes under pressure. Adjectives are not mechanics. Test: 'speaks softly,' 'blunt,' 'uses technical jargon' score 0–40 — these are labels, not instructions a writer can type from. 'Clipped, verbless fragments that grow longer and more formal when he is cornered' scores 70+ — a writer knows exactly what to produce. Distinctness between characters is NOT required and must not be scored: two characters may legitimately share a similar voice (siblings, same upbringing). Judge each voice solely on whether it is concrete enough to imitate.

criteria.name: downstream_utility
criteria.description: Downstream stages can consume the premise without hitting a broken reference or a placeholder. protagonist_id resolves to a character in the list. appearance_tags have concrete values, not 'unknown' or empty. Each tone_directive ties to a specific dialogue behavior, not just a mood word. The setting's physical_description is concrete enough to generate consistent images. Test: any unresolved id, placeholder value, or mood-word-without-behavior brings the score below 50; a premise where every field is directly usable by the next stage scores 70+.
